description: Test your knowledge of Minerals, electrolytes, Water and Acid base balance.

cards.text: Compare bioavailability of haem iron vs non-haem iron and explain the mechanism for non-haem iron absorption.
cards.answer: Haem iron (Fe²⁺ from meat) has 20-30% bioavailability via HCP1 receptor. Non-haem iron (Fe³⁺ from vegetables) must be reduced to Fe²⁺ by ferrireductase (Dcytb), then transported by DMT1; enhanced by Vitamin C but inhibited by phytates, oxalates, and tannins.

tip.tip: HCP1 = Haem Carrier Protein; Dcytb = ferrireductase; remember meat > vegetables for iron bioavailability

cards.text: How does hepcidin regulate iron homeostasis and what happens in chronic disease?
cards.answer: Hepcidin binds ferroportin to internalise it, blocking iron release from enterocytes, macrophages, and hepatocytes. High hepcidin in chronic disease traps iron intracellularly, causing anaemia of chronic disease despite adequate body stores.

tip.tip: Hepcidin = 'iron lock' hormone; high hepcidin = iron trapped = anaemia despite normal stores

cards.text: List the three stages of iron deficiency development with key laboratory findings.
cards.answer: Stage 1 (Iron depletion): Serum ferritin <12 µg/L, no anaemia. Stage 2 (Iron-deficient erythropoiesis): TIBC↑, transferrin saturation <20%, mild microcytosis. Stage 3 (IDA): Hb↓, microcytic hypochromic RBCs (MCV <80, MCH <27), raised RDW.

tip.tip: Remember: ferritin first → then saturation falls → finally haemoglobin drops; ABC = Always Before Crisis

cards.text: What are the classic RBC morphology findings and diagnostic hallmark of iron deficiency anaemia?
cards.answer: Microcytic hypochromic RBCs with pencil cells and target cells on blood film. Diagnostic panel shows: ferritin↓, serum iron↓, TIBC↑, transferrin saturation <20%, RDW↑ (anisocytosis).

tip.tip: Pencil cells = thin, pale RBCs; target cells = bull's-eye appearance; RDW = variation in size

cards.text: Describe the triple axis regulation of serum calcium and the opposing actions of PTH and calcitonin.
cards.answer: Low Ca²⁺ triggers PTH → increases renal Ca reabsorption, bone resorption, and renal 1α-hydroxylase (↑ calcitriol) → intestinal Ca absorption. Calcitonin (from thyroid C-cells) opposes PTH by inhibiting osteoclasts and reducing calcium reabsorption.

tip.tip: PTH = calcium raiser; Calcitonin = calcium lowerer; calcitriol = active Vitamin D (1,25-OH)

cards.text: List the clinical signs of hypocalcaemia and explain the pathophysiology of tetany and Chvostek/Trousseau signs.
cards.answer: Hypocalcaemia causes paraesthesiae, muscle cramps, tetany (carpal spasm), positive Chvostek sign (facial nerve tap → twitch), and Trousseau sign (BP cuff inflation → carpal spasm). These occur because low Ca²⁺ increases neuromuscular irritability and spontaneous firing.

tip.tip: Chvostek = tap face; Trousseau = squeeze arm; both = spasm from low Ca²⁺ hyperexcitability

cards.text: What is the significance of serum ferritin and how is it interpreted in different clinical scenarios?
cards.answer: Serum ferritin is the best marker of iron stores. Low ferritin (<12 µg/L) = iron deficiency. High ferritin indicates iron overload (haemochromatosis) OR acute inflammation/infection/liver disease. Always interpret with inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR).

tip.tip: Ferritin = iron storage gauge; rises with inflammation mimicking iron overload — check CRP!

cards.text: Describe total body iron distribution and identify the clinically most important pool.
cards.answer: Total body iron ~3.5-4 g: ~65% in haemoglobin (most clinically important), ~10% in myoglobin/enzymes, ~20-25% stored as ferritin/haemosiderin, ~0.1% in plasma bound to transferrin. Haemoglobin is the critical functional pool.

tip.tip: 2/3 in Hb + 1/3 split between myoglobin/enzymes/storage; only 0.1% circulates = why serum ferritin reflects total stores
